The musician opens up to PEOPLE about returning to the stage for Elle World and the challenges she faced with her mixed-race identity. Amid the sea of blonde pop stars in the early aughts like Britney Spears, Christina Aguilera, Mandy Moore and Jessica Simpson came Hoku. If you were a millennial between 2000 and 2001, it would have been near-impossible to be unfamiliar with Hoku’s first single Another Dumb Blonde or her second bubbly juggernaut Perfect Day, which became the infectious intro song to the 2001 hit comedy Legally Blonde. But not long after releasing her self-titled debut album, just as the Hawaiian-born singer was blossoming as a pop star, she walked away from the spotlight. I did mourn that things were not different, and I mourned that around 21, 22, my dream was over... but now I just feel so much gratitude because I stepped out, Hoku, now 45, says, adjusting the flower from her ear on a Zoom call from her home in Los Angeles. Out of the public eye, Hoku (born Hoku Christian Ho) spent the last two decades raising her three kids — a 17-year-old daughter, a 15-year-old son and a 12-year-old son — living a quiet life and quietly writing music. For a moment in 2018, she returned with the Christian EP Called by Name and the single Greater in 2020. But she’s since stepped back from her faith as well. It stopped feeling authentic, she says. In June, for the first time in years, Hoku made a rare appearance and performance at Elle World ahead of the premiere of the prequel series Elle. And now, she’s eyeing a comeback. Below, Hoku opens up to PEOPLE about why she left the music industry, leaving her faith behind and the surprising celebrity fans she’s made over the years. 

PEOPLE: How did Legally Blonde and its use of Perfect Day change your life?

HOKU: Perfect Day came at the end of what became the end of my music career, but it was this lovely little period where the song was really connecting with people. I was touring it, and then in the movie it was a bit of an afterthought for my label. There was a lot of like, Well, this movie’s probably not going to be that. It was kind of low-budget; it was a female-led movie. But it ended up being the most defining song of my career, and I feel so thankful for that. The movie itself is such a special movie and so in line with who I am as a person. It feels really good to have that be such a big part of my legacy.

PEOPLE: In the early aughts it felt like you were really gaining momentum and then you disappeared. What happened between you and your record label after the release of Perfect Day?

HOKU: Perfect Day was meant to be the lead single for my follow-up album, and it was associated with the movie. The movie did a lot more than people were expecting. So I was touring it, performing it live, but behind the scenes, there were conversations about my next album. And by then, my label and I ... specifically one person at the label; he was a creep. He was exactly one of those people that you hear about, and he was really in charge of everything with my music. There had been a lot of pressure from everyone — him included — to sexualize my image, be willing to put out the vibe that I was down for whatever to all these radio people. I loved the music. I loved the singing. I loved the performing. It had been my dream, but there was just this hunted feeling; this I’m prey amongst predators kind of feeling. That was just how the industry worked back then. So, I was already kind of thinking to myself, I don’t know if this is worth it for me anymore. Then, this guy made an ultimatum, and was like, You will do X, Y, and Z. I’m sick of you teasing me enough, or I’m going to bury your record. And I was like, Okay. I got up, walked out of that meeting and that was it. That was the end of that. The spin I put on it was that it wasn’t in line with my faith, which at the time was very true. I was a very devoted Christian at that time. I’ve since stepped out of my faith, but that was true to some degree. It wasn’t something I was comfortable with. I was 18, 19, 20, 21. I was just barely coming into my own sexuality at that point. [I] didn’t feel like marketing that to the masses, but ultimately it did come down to an ultimatum. So I walked away.

 PEOPLE: From what I understand, you were also married at the time, and the record label wanted you to pretend that you weren’t. Tell me about that.

HOKU: Yes. That was the big secret of my music career — that I was married the whole time! I’m still married to him. We still love each other very much. We just celebrated 27 years. I realized that’s not normal for young married people to be like that. But I do feel really lucky. At the time it felt so unjust. But in retrospect, I do understand a little bit of, We’re not going to market that this teenybopper pop star is married. What bothered me was that there was this guy [at] the label [that] was like, You need to get divorced. How long ago did you get married? Can we annul this? That was one of the first meetings we had. Things just never really improved from there. I wouldn’t travel or tour without [my husband] because he very much felt like my protector during a time when I was feeling very hunted, like I was saying. They ended up being like, Okay, well, we might as well give him a job. So then he was working alongside my tour manager during my last summer that I was touring. He ended up getting into the business side of things, but in the beginning he was just my guy. (PEOPLE has reached out to Universal Music, the parent company of Interscope/Geffen Records, for comment.).

PEOPLE: You ended up walking away from your pop career. At this juncture, do you have any regrets about that?

HOKU: Not at this juncture. I did then. Not that I would have stayed in the environment I was in, but I did mourn that things were not different, and I mourned that around 21, 22, my dream was over. This thing I’d worked for my whole life since I was 11 and singing on my dad’s show … there was a lot of mourning throughout in the interim time, but now I just feel so much gratitude because I stepped out. I was able to raise my family in peace because I had gotten out of the game before anything got too out of hand. I left before the whole paparazzi tabloid culture was really a thing. I’m watching all these girls just getting out of limos at parties, trying to go grocery shopping, having these purposely unflattering photos taken of them and that whole critical attitude towards women’s bodies; I was able to sidestep that. I just got to go live my life in relative peace, so that was nice. I don’t regret it at all now. 

PEOPLE: In the early 2000s, the typical mainstream pop star was white and blonde for the most part. As a multiracial artist who is a part of the AAPI community, were there any pressures you felt at the time?

 HOKU: I felt like I’m very white-passing. I’m blonde; I have pale skin. Everyone in my family is not. I’m the white sheep of my family. So, I’ve always had a little bit of a feeling already that I don’t belong in my culture. I don’t look associated with the culture I identify most with, which would be my local Hawaiian and Asian mixed culture that exists there. I grew up feeling very connected to that, but also having people yell at me in the water like, Hey haole, get off my wave. I’m like, I’m one of you. So there’s always been a little bit of sadness around not being able to be more visually connected to my culture. There is always a little bit of imposter syndrome, this low-key sense of, Gosh, look how pale I am. Look how blonde I am. Maybe I don’t have a right to represent my culture. Maybe I don’t have a right to be saying that I am Asian or Hawaiian. But that was also very much a part of my marketing. It was a lot about [being] Hawaiian because my dad is very associated with Hawaii, and less about [being] Asian, even though my dad raised us very Asian. His dad was a Chinese chef. What I felt the most was: Is it okay that I want to represent this? Am I allowed? But also I was very proud of the fact that my Hawaiianness was on the forefront, and that I was able to represent home. Because the people of Hawaii were so excited that one of their own was there and making it in the industry. There’s probably, at that time, this weird, subconscious sense of imposter syndrome around claiming parts of my ethnicity that I didn’t visually represent in my mind. I think now [that] I looked more Asian than I thought at the time. As I look back at my life, I’m like — it was just the coloring and the kind of childhood weirdness that I hadn’t really processed yet.

PEOPLE: That’s really challenging. Thank you for sharing that.

HOKU: It’s weird. It’s been an interesting journey throughout my life. Because even after I walked away from my pop music, there was a hot minute where I was trying to do some acting. And I just remember one of the roles I lost out on was the role Hilary Duff got in Cheaper by the Dozen. I was far along, and once she got the part, I was like, Well, duh, she looks like Bonnie Hunt and Steve Martin’s daughter. I don’t really. I wasn’t getting called in for Asian roles or Hawaiian roles; I was getting called in for these [roles like] You’re the cheerleader that gets killed. You’re the bimbo at the party. And then I was just like, Well, I don’t fit here either. I never felt like I really fit, and I feel like it’s actually been the interim time that I’ve really made peace with the fact that, no, I am these things. This is my culture, these are my people, this is who I am. I’ve made that journey over the years, but definitely had not at 18, 19, 20, 21. 

PEOPLE: Your highest-charting single was Another Dumb Blonde and not Perfect Day. Does that remain surprising for you?

HOKU: It doesn’t [surprise me] because of where the industry was at the time. It was the end of the CD era and the beginning of the downloads era. [With] Another Dumb Blonde, I kept being told, Oh yeah, it’s got this many CDs sold, but then it has this many downloads on Napster or whatever. The idea was if it weren’t for these downloads, you would have had so much more. Certainly by the time Perfect Day had come out, there was a lot more of that. 

PEOPLE: You have three kids now. What do they think of your career as a pop star? 

HOKU: They’ve known about it since around elementary school [with] other people at their school, the moms, putting it together. So, it’s been a part of their lives in theory, but there wasn’t really an opportunity for them to really understand what it was like or really wrap their head around it. But then when I got to do this Elle World event, I took them all with me, and they got to see me in my pop-star mode performing my songs. That was a really cool moment for me and for us to be able to share that. I think my kids all appreciate my pop stuff, but I wouldn’t say that they listen to it a ton. If I had to pick one, they all love How Do I Feel (The Burrito Song). I don’t know why. Since they got to watch me perform, I noticed them listening to it a lot more often, but they prefer the songs that I just play around the house that I’ve been writing during their lifetime.

PEOPLE: Between 2001 and 2018, were you focusing on raising your kids, or did you start another career?

HOKU: No, I just kind of focused on raising my kids. I had the luxury of being able to do that, and I really wanted to just devote myself to that, so I was lucky that I got to do that.

PEOPLE: In 2018, you released a Christian EP, as well as a single in 2020. What prompted you to step away from your faith, and when did that happen?

HOKU: That Christian album was the last gasp of me trying to make sense of what I believed. When I became a Christian, it was in Hawaii and in this sort of hippie way. It was like Jesus is love, man. I really just resonated with that message of inclusivity. In Hawaii, there is a lot of inclusivity racially [and in terms of] sexual orientation, and I was lucky in California to be in spaces that still fostered that sense of inclusivity. But as I saw the church, the Big C church devolve into this place that didn’t at all feel centered around what had connected me to it in the first place, I started to step back and question some of the things that I had been believing over time. I think of my faith now as an expansion of what I used to believe. I believe in a higher power. I believe in the universe. I call it whatever I feel like in the moment. But I think that Christianity has become very much about labels [and] boxes. It stopped feeling authentic. I didn’t feel like I had to be so sure of everything. I’m okay with the gray area now. I still have so much love for people in my life that are still in that world, but I feel like I’ve evolved a little bit past that in my personal beliefs. It was definitely a journey, and at times very painful, because not everyone in my life was still my friend or still loving me once I made this decision. But ultimately I have to live authentically and be true to what I actually think and feel instead of trying to remain part of some club. 

PEOPLE: Back in the early 2000s, what was your favorite celebrity encounter you had?

HOKU: There are so many lovely people. Rachael Leigh Cook and I would always run into each other at events, and every time we would see each other, we were like, Oh, hi. It was always nice to see her and catch up with her. I was obviously on the tour circuit that included a lot of the pop artists. So Mandy [Moore’s] manager and my manager were friends and then Jessica Simpson was dating Nick Lachey, so then I did the 98 Degrees special and we were in the same tour circuit. We were all very friendly, but I think there’s a little more competition there, but not in any overt way. Jennifer Love Hewitt and I had a great encounter, [and] Kobe Bryant. He was just so gracious. Lance Bass [and] Chris Kirkpatrick were very sweet. So, no ill will or bad blood. We were all just kind of out there doing our thing and happy to see each other.

PEOPLE: Perfect Day has had so much longevity, and especially on TikTok there’s been celebs and fans making videos. Earlier this year, for instance, Hilary Duff made one when she was making her return to the stage, which is funny because I know a remix of Perfect Day was used in Lizzie McGuire. Is there a favorite fan or celeb TikTok video or edit that you have featuring the song?

HOKU: I mean, definitely Hilary. That was just so cute, and I appreciated that homage as she was making her reentry back into music. It got the most legs, for sure, that I’ve seen.

PEOPLE: Throughout the last two decades, is there a celebrity fan of Perfect Day that’s surprised you?

HOKU: At the Elle World event, I found out that Bowen Yang and Matt Rogers were going to be hosting the panel, and I was so excited. I love them, and I love Bowen. I watched SNL when he was on it, and I just think he’s so funny. He’s Asian, so I was just like, Oh, it’s one of my people. And in the limo ride over or the Escalade ride over, I turned back to my family [and] was like, You guys, I think I might die if Bowen Yang knows who I am. That would be just the dream if he knew who I was. So, when I get there and we’re getting ready for the whole photo op, Bowen is right in front of me getting ready. [The person with me] was like, Do you want to meet Bowen? And I was like, Oh my God, yes. So then she [says], Oh, hey, this is Hoku. This is Bowen. And then his face was just blank. And I was like, Oh my God, okay, this is going to be so awkward. And then he goes, Sorry, what was your name? And I’m like, Hoku. Then his face lit up. He’s like, Hoku. Oh my God, you’re Hoku. He goes, You’re the person I was most excited to see. And I was like, You’re the person I was most excited to see. Anyway, we’re friends now. He’s basically my bestie. Then Matt was so sweet. That was a really cool moment. It was [also] fun to talk to Reese [Witherspoon] again because we’d spent a day in London together shooting this music video. She was just so excited that I was there and clearly such a fan of the song and so proud that it was connected to Elle and everything. There’s a video of her while I was performing, singing along on Perfect Day. She’s really championed it. Over the years, she’s done videos with Perfect Day in it. I’m just really grateful that she’s embraced my connection to it as well. 

PEOPLE: This year Bowen and Matt performed Only Hope with Mandy Moore at the Las Culturistas Awards, which is incredible. What if they did something similar for Perfect Day with you?

HOKU: Oh my God, that would be amazing. Let’s just both put that out in the universe. 

PEOPLE: I’ve heard you’re back in the recording studio. Can you tell me what you’ve been working on?

HOKU: I’m putting together an album based on a bunch of songs that I think would really be good for [it]. There’s stuff that I would like to have out in the world. Any interaction I have on social media, it’s like, When’s the comeback? When’s the new music? And there were a lot of years where I wasn’t really writing songs that would feel like they fit into the Hoku universe. Writing is how I process things and get things out of my body, and so, for a long time there were songs that were me just trying to process who I was after being a pop star was over, and then who I was as a mom. And for a long time, it was who I was in my faith before I stepped away from that. The timing is really perfect because over the last many years I’ve been in this really joyful, open-hearted state. My kids are in their teens and pre-teens. We’ve had a lot of fun. They’re great kids, and there’s a little bit of that sense of being able to step back and just enjoy your handiwork. I was already gearing up [for new music] before I was reached out to for the Elle World event. I was like, Oh my God, this is perfect timing. Because I was already getting ready to, in my own way, think of how I was going to relaunch, and this just gave me a huge springboard. 

PEOPLE: Are you signed to a label at this point?

HOKU: No, I’m not signed to a label at this point. I was kind of trying to see how much I could do on my own. My label experience wasn’t great. I know things are much different now, but I haven’t really pursued that yet. I’d imagine at a certain point that might be necessary, but there’s a lot that you can do now without a label. It’s something I’m open to but haven’t begun to pursue. 

PEOPLE: Have you been asked — or would you — create a song for the TV show Elle?

HOKU: I’d be open to any and everything like that. I think I hid for a lot of years and just enjoyed my anonymity, enjoyed the peace I was able to give my kids, but we’re all good now. Now I feel more freed up energetically to put all of that towards getting back into spreading joy to the world through my music and bringing some of that joy and nostalgia back. I’m doing songwriting stuff behind the scenes. I’ve been doing that a little bit over the years and stuff, so that’s already something I’m definitely in. It would just be fun. 

PEOPLE: Do you have plans to tour in the future?

HOKU: I would love to tour. I’d be super down to do that. Bring it on.

<p id="mntl-sc-block_16-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> The pair also recalled forming Sugarland back in 2002. “We were in Atlanta, and we had each had our own indie careers, and Kristian had some major label career,” said Nettles. “But we were writing at the time, we were doing our own things, and we sort of started as an Atlanta supergroup.”
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_17-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_18-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> Bush explained, “No one believed us that we were making country music... So, I went out and I got a hat on eBay to convince my friends.”
</p>

<p id="mntl-sc-block_20-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> Since forming Sugarland, the pair notched chart-topping country hits with “Want To,” “Settlin,” “All I Want to Do,” “Already Gone” and “It Happens.”

<p id="mntl-sc-block_23-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> This week, Nettles and Bush announced the upcoming Ride or Die Tour to celebrate the 20th anniversary of Sugarland’s <em>Enjoy the Ride </em>album.
</p>

<p id="mntl-sc-block_25-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> “This was a huge record for us,” said Nettles on <em>Today</em>. “This was a big turning point in our career. I mean, our debut album was great, but then this was really when people started to catch onto what we were doing.”
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_26-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_27-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> The Ride or Die Tour runs through October and November with shows throughout North America. Ticket information is available at Sugarland’s website.

gold_text: Nettles and Bush spoke to Today about why their creative partnership works as they prepare for a tour celebrating 20 years of Enjoy the Ride. What keeps Sugarland a successful duo? Jennifer Nettles and Kristian Bush appeared on the Thursday, Aug. 11 episode of the Today show to discuss their upcoming Ride or Die Tour and the secret to their decades-long creative partnership. I think like any relationship, you keep it fresh and you communicate, said Nettles, 51, of working with Bush, 56. It doesnt matter if its family. It doesnt matter if its intimate. It doesnt matter if its creative, whatever. Keep it fresh. We do, obviously other things, added the Stay vocalist, highlighting Bushs work with Megan Moroney. Nettles, on the other hand, recently starred as the titular character in an off-Broadway production of Giulia: The Poison Queen of Palermo. Bush said of their working relationship, We are a unique duo in that almost every single time weve sat down to do anything, maybe even in the dressing room before we walked up here, we will come up with ideas on the spot that work almost every time. The pair also recalled forming Sugarland back in 2002. We were in Atlanta, and we had each had our own indie careers, and Kristian had some major label career, said Nettles. But we were writing at the time, we were doing our own things, and we sort of started as an Atlanta supergroup. Bush explained, No one believed us that we were making country music... So, I went out and I got a hat on eBay to convince my friends. Since forming Sugarland, the pair notched chart-topping country hits with Want To, Settlin, All I Want to Do, Already Gone and It Happens. This week, Nettles and Bush announced the upcoming Ride or Die Tour to celebrate the 20th anniversary of Sugarlands Enjoy the Ride album. This was a huge record for us, said Nettles on Today. This was a big turning point in our career. I mean, our debut album was great, but then this was really when people started to catch onto what we were doing. The Ride or Die Tour runs through October and November with shows throughout North America. Ticket information is available at Sugarlands website.

<p id="mntl-sc-block_2-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> The much-anticipated return of Starbucks’ Unicorn Frappuccino is almost upon us.
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_3-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_4-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> The coffee giant <a href="https://people.com/starbucks-announces-when-unicorn-frappuccino-will-return-12023300" data-component="link" data-source="inlineLink" data-type="internalLink" data-ordinal="1">revealed</a> last month that the blended pink and blue creation would be back on menus for just “one magical weekend,” beginning on Aug. 15.
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_5-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_6-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> PEOPLE got an early taste of the colorful beverage, which Starbucks says features the original recipe from 2017 — the year it gained viral fame.
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_7-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_8-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> “The fan-favorite sweet and tart blend of creamy mango flavors, tangy blue drizzle, whipped cream, and pink and blue topping is back exactly as remembered,” the company said in a release shared with PEOPLE. “A swirl of the cup reveals color-changing enchantment and a transformation of flavors.”
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_9-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>

<p id="mntl-sc-block_28-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> Starbucks describes Chaider as “a cozy twist on chai for fall” with flavors of cinnamon and sweet spice. The drink can be ordered hot or iced.

</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_31-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_32-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> “Banana is having a moment and it’s joining the Starbucks menu,” Starbucks said in a press release shared with PEOPLE. “As banana flavors continue popping up everywhere, Starbucks is expanding its banana-inspired lineup with two new beverages inspired by freshly baked banana bread.”

<p id="mntl-sc-block_34-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> The new Iced Banana Bread Latte and Iced Banana Bread Chai feature banana, cinnamon and brown sugar flavors “to create dessert-like notes reminiscent of warm baked treats,” Starbucks said, adding that they’ll be available past the season.

gold_text: The pink and blue beverage will land on menus Saturday, Aug. 15. The much-anticipated return of Starbucks’ Unicorn Frappuccino is almost upon us. The coffee giant revealed last month that the blended pink and blue creation would be back on menus for just one magical weekend, beginning on Aug. 15. PEOPLE got an early taste of the colorful beverage, which Starbucks says features the original recipe from 2017 — the year it gained viral fame. The fan-favorite sweet and tart blend of creamy mango flavors, tangy blue drizzle, whipped cream, and pink and blue topping is back exactly as remembered, the company said in a release shared with PEOPLE. A swirl of the cup reveals color-changing enchantment and a transformation of flavors. For fans who missed the combination of tropical sweetness and a sour-candy kick, the creamy drink likely won’t disappoint. The bold fruity flavors and striking swirls reminded us of why it became a social media sensation nearly a decade ago. The Unicorn Frappuccino was served at Coachella Music Festival this past April, sparking nostalgia for the color-changing concoction. Later this month, Starbucks will bring back the Pumpkin Spice Latte as part of its fall menu. The pumpkin lineup, available starting Aug. 25, also includes a new Iced Pumpkin Cream Shaken Espresso, Pumpkin Spice Chai and Iced Pumpkin Cream Matcha. The Pumpkin Cream Cold Brew, Iced Pumpkin Cream Chai and Pumpkin Spice Frappuccino will be making a comeback. This year’s autumn offerings also include pecan drinks, banana bread-inspired drinks and a new Chaider item that combines chai and cider flavors. Starbucks describes Chaider as a cozy twist on chai for fall with flavors of cinnamon and sweet spice. The drink can be ordered hot or iced. The Pecan Cortado, Iced Pecan Crunch Latte and Pecan Crunch Latte, with a signature combination of nutty flavors, rich brown-buttery notes and baking spices, will all return to coffeehouses. Banana is having a moment and it’s joining the Starbucks menu, Starbucks said in a press release shared with PEOPLE. As banana flavors continue popping up everywhere, Starbucks is expanding its banana-inspired lineup with two new beverages inspired by freshly baked banana bread. The new Iced Banana Bread Latte and Iced Banana Bread Chai feature banana, cinnamon and brown sugar flavors to create dessert-like notes reminiscent of warm baked treats, Starbucks said, adding that they’ll be available past the season.

<div class="mntl-sc-block-universal-callout__body"><ul><li>Delta Air Lines says an unauthorized Wi-Fi network appeared briefly during a flight from Las Vegas to Atlanta</li><li>The airline deactivated in-flight Wi-Fi for 30 minutes and confirmed no critical systems were affected</li><li>The incident occurred after a major hacker convention in Las Vegas and is being investigated by federal authorities</li></ul></div>
</div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_2-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> Authorities are investigating a potential cybersecurity incident that occurred during a Delta Air Lines flight after an “unauthorized Wi-Fi network” appeared on board. 
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_3-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_4-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> A Delta Air Lines spokesperson tells PEOPLE the company is investigating flight 591, which flew from Las Vegas to Atlanta on Monday, Aug. 10. The company says initial findings point to an “unauthorized Wi-Fi network, which was not provided, operated or supplied by Delta,” that appeared for a short time during the flight. 
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_5-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_6-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> According to <a href="https://app.airframes.io/messages/7299479024" data-type="" data-component="link" data-source="inlineLink" data-ordinal="1" rel="noopener noreferrer nofollow" target="_blank">Airframes.io</a>, a community-driven open aviation data network, pilots sent a text-based message to air traffic control claiming a passenger “created a scam Wifi called Delta Wifi Fast.”
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_7-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_8-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> They added: “We believe they are trying to scam the [other passengers.]”
</p>

<p id="mntl-sc-block_15-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> The ”safety of the flight was never in question and no aircraft operating systems were affected,” Delta’s statement addressing the incident says. gold_text: Delta crew members shut off in-flight Wi-Fi mid-flight after discovering a rogue network allegedly named Delta Wifi Fast on a flight from Las Vegas. Authorities are investigating a potential cybersecurity incident that occurred during a Delta Air Lines flight after an unauthorized Wi-Fi network appeared on board. A Delta Air Lines spokesperson tells PEOPLE the company is investigating flight 591, which flew from Las Vegas to Atlanta on Monday, Aug. 10. The company says initial findings point to an unauthorized Wi-Fi network, which was not provided, operated or supplied by Delta, that appeared for a short time during the flight. According to Airframes.io, a community-driven open aviation data network, pilots sent a text-based message to air traffic control claiming a passenger created a scam Wifi called Delta Wifi Fast. They added: We believe they are trying to scam the [other passengers.]. In response, the cabin crew deactivated the aircraft’s Wi-Fi functionality for approximately 30 minutes, Delta reports. The safety of the flight was never in question and no aircraft operating systems were affected, Delta’s statement addressing the incident says. The spokesperson added there was no hack of any Delta system, including the in-flight Wi-Fi. We will partner with federal law enforcement and aviation regulators to ensure the incident is thoroughly investigated. A spokesperson for the Federal Aviation Administration said the department is aware and looking into the report, but notes that a breach of an onboard Wi-Fi system would not affect an airplane’s critical flight-safety systems. The FBI National Press Office tells PEOPLE it is aware of the reports and is in contact with local and corporate partners on the matter. However, no additional information was available at this time. In its message shared with PEOPLE, Delta Air Lines pointed out that large cybersecurity conferences were held in Las Vegas this past weekend. The events included DEF CON, an annual hacker convention, which took place from Aug. 6 to 9. Experts have previously warned about evil twin attacks, in which someone creates a fraudulent access point that mimics a legitimate Wi-Fi network. When victims connect to the system, hackers can then use tools to intercept information, steal data or otherwise exploit the device.

<div id="article-content_1-0" class="comp article-content mntl-block"><div id="mntl-sc-page_1-0" class="comp mntl-sc-page mntl-block structured-content" data-sc-sticky-offset="90" data-sc-ad-label-height="24" data-sc-ad-track-spacing="100" data-sc-min-track-height="250" data-sc-max-track-height="600" data-sc-breakpoint="50em" data-sc-load-immediate="4" data-sc-content-positions="[1, 1250, 1550, 1950, 2350, 2750, 3150, 3550, 3950]" data-bind-scroll-on-start="true"><div id="mntl-sc-block_1-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block people-sc-block-callout mntl-sc-block-universal-callout theme-needtoknow" data-tracking-id="mntl-sc-block-callout" data-tracking-container="true"> <h3 class="mntl-sc-block-universal-callout__heading">NEED TO KNOW</h3>
<div class="mntl-sc-block-universal-callout__body"><ul><li>Nicole Kidman has opened up about what it was like marrying Tom Cruise at age 22 and being thrust into the spotlight at a young age</li><li>The actress told <em>British Vogue</em> that she was warned the marriage could affect her career, but decided to prioritize love over professional concerns at the time</li><li>The pair were married for over a decade, adopted two children, and starred in multiple films together</li></ul></div>
</div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_2-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> <a class="null" href="https://people.com/tag/nicole-kidman/" data-component="link" data-source="inlineLink" data-type="internalLink" data-ordinal="1" rel="null">Nicole Kidman</a> is looking back on her marriage to <a class="null" href="https://people.com/tag/tom-cruise/" data-component="link" data-source="inlineLink" data-type="internalLink" data-ordinal="2" rel="null">Tom Cruise</a> as a “completely natural” part of her life. 
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_3-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_4-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> The 59-year-old Oscar winner made rare comments about her marriage to the action star in a new cover story for <a class="null" href="https://www.vogue.co.uk/article/nicole-kidman-british-vogue-interview" data-component="link" data-source="inlineLink" data-type="externalLink" data-ordinal="1" rel="null noopener" target="_blank"><em>British Vogue</em></a><em>,</em> after the pair tied the knot on Christmas Eve in 1990. 
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_5-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_6-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> Sharing that she feels very “comfortable” at high-profile events like fashion shows and red carpets, Kidman said, “You have to remember literally, because of who I married at such a young age, I was thrust into it since I was 22. [My life has been] more time like that than not. My memory of it not being that is quite blurry, because I was really young.”
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_7-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_8-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> Remarking on getting “married so young” to Cruise, the <em>Practical Magic</em> star noted, “Suddenly I was 22, 23 years old and I had this huge movie star husband. But it just seemed completely natural. We just fell madly in love and it was that simple.” 
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_9-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"><div id="mm-ads-native-fluid_1-0" class="comp mm-ads-native-fluid mm-ads-native " style="--native-ad-height: auto" data-right-rail-index="2"><div id="mm-ads-native__adunit_1-0" class="comp mm-ads-native__adunit mm-ads-gpt-dynamic-adunit mm-ads-gpt-adunit scads-to-load gpt native js-immediate-ad js-immediate-ad-loaded">

<p id="mntl-sc-block_11-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> Kidman said she was warned against the union at the time. 
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_12-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_13-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> “I remember people saying to me, ‘OK, well this is really going to affect your career,’ ” she recalled to the outlet. “I’m like, ‘I don’t care. I’m in love. I want to be married.’ And then I was his ‘wife’ and they were like, ‘See, we told you.’ I’m like, ‘So what? I wasn’t meant to marry the man I love? Of course I’ll throw my career away. I don’t care.’ ”
</p>

<p id="mntl-sc-block_17-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> Kidman and Cruise stayed together for more than a decade, before they officially divorced in August 2001. gold_text: The actress told ‘British Vogue’ that she was warned the marriage could affect her career, but decided to prioritize love over professional concerns at the time. Nicole Kidman is looking back on her marriage to Tom Cruise as a completely natural part of her life. The 59-year-old Oscar winner made rare comments about her marriage to the action star in a new cover story for British Vogue, after the pair tied the knot on Christmas Eve in 1990. Sharing that she feels very comfortable at high-profile events like fashion shows and red carpets, Kidman said, You have to remember literally, because of who I married at such a young age, I was thrust into it since I was 22. [My life has been] more time like that than not. My memory of it not being that is quite blurry, because I was really young. Remarking on getting married so young to Cruise, the Practical Magic star noted, Suddenly I was 22, 23 years old and I had this huge movie star husband. But it just seemed completely natural. We just fell madly in love and it was that simple. Kidman said she was warned against the union at the time. I remember people saying to me, ‘OK, well this is really going to affect your career,’  she recalled to the outlet. I’m like, ‘I don’t care. I’m in love. I want to be married.’ And then I was his ‘wife’ and they were like, ‘See, we told you.’ I’m like, ‘So what? I wasn’t meant to marry the man I love? Of course I’ll throw my career away. I don’t care.’. Kidman and Cruise stayed together for more than a decade, before they officially divorced in August 2001. The pair — who adopted children Bella, 33, and Connor, 31 — originally met on the set of the 1990 film Days of Thunder. They went on to star together in several films including Ron Howard’s Far and Away (1992) and Stanley Kubrick’s Eyes Wide Shut (1999). Reflecting on her marriage to Cruise during a 2013 Vanity Fair interview, Kidman previously said of their split, I had a lot of time alone, which was really, really good, because I was a child, really, when I got married. And I needed to grow up. She went on to marry singer Keith Urban in 2006. The former pair announced their split in September 2025 after 19 years of marriage. They share daughters Sunday Rose, 18, and Faith Margaret, 15, together. In 2018, Kidman revealed in an interview with New York Magazine why she didn’t like to talk about her marriage to Cruise. Being married to Tom Cruise at 22 is something I’m always reluctant to talk about, because I’m married now to the man who is my great love, and it almost feels disrespectful, Kidman said at the time of her then-husband Urban. That said, I got married very young, but it definitely wasn’t power for me — it was protection, she continued. I married for love, but being married to an extremely powerful man kept me from being sexually harassed. I would work, but I was still very much cocooned. So when I came out of it at 32, 33, it’s almost like I had to grow up.

<div id="article-content_1-0" class="comp article-content mntl-block"><div id="mntl-sc-page_1-0" class="comp mntl-sc-page mntl-block structured-content" data-sc-sticky-offset="90" data-sc-ad-label-height="24" data-sc-ad-track-spacing="100" data-sc-min-track-height="250" data-sc-max-track-height="600" data-sc-breakpoint="50em" data-sc-load-immediate="4" data-sc-content-positions="[1, 1250, 1550, 1950, 2350, 2750, 3150, 3550, 3950]" data-bind-scroll-on-start="true"><div id="mntl-sc-block_1-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block people-sc-block-callout mntl-sc-block-universal-callout theme-needtoknow" data-tracking-id="mntl-sc-block-callout" data-tracking-container="true"> <h3 class="mntl-sc-block-universal-callout__heading">NEED TO KNOW</h3>
<div class="mntl-sc-block-universal-callout__body"><ul><li>Demi Lovato spoke about celebrating her first wedding anniversary with Jordan “Jutes” Lutes as she attended the <em>Camp Rock 3 </em>premiere on Monday, Aug. 10</li></ul><ul><li>“When you’re able to communicate with each other what you need, what you want, it creates a safe space for the two of you to share your feelings with one another,” the actress tells PEOPLE</li><li>The couple wed in May 2025 in California, with Lovato wearing a custom Vivienne Westwood gown</li></ul></div>
</div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_2-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> <a class="null" href="https://people.com/tag/demi-lovato/" data-component="link" data-source="inlineLink" data-type="internalLink" data-ordinal="1" rel="null">Demi Lovato</a> is reflecting on the secret to her happy marriage!
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_3-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_4-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> While attending the <a class="null" href="https://people.com/demi-lovato-jonas-brothers-reunite-camp-rock-3-premiere-los-angeles-12056852" data-component="link" data-source="inlineLink" data-type="internalLink" data-ordinal="1" rel="null">premiere of </a><em><a class="null" href="https://people.com/demi-lovato-jonas-brothers-reunite-camp-rock-3-premiere-los-angeles-12056852" data-component="link" data-source="inlineLink" data-type="internalLink" data-ordinal="2" rel="null">Camp Rock 3</a></em><em> </em>at the Walt Disney Studio lot in Burbank, Calif., on Monday, Aug. 10, Lovato — who is <a class="null" href="https://people.com/demi-lovato-confirms-surprise-cameo-camp-rock-3-jonas-brothers-12053220" data-component="link" data-source="inlineLink" data-type="internalLink" data-ordinal="3" rel="null">reprising her role</a> of Mitchie Torres, as well as acting as executive producer alongside the <a class="null" href="https://people.com/tag/jonas-brothers/" data-component="link" data-source="inlineLink" data-type="internalLink" data-ordinal="4" rel="null">Jonas Brothers</a>, in the upcoming film — spoke to PEOPLE about her recent one-year anniversary.
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_5-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_6-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> Lovato, 33, who <a class="null" href="https://people.com/demi-lovato-marries-jordan-jutes-lutes-wedding-8347793" data-component="link" data-source="inlineLink" data-type="internalLink" data-ordinal="1" rel="null">tied the knot</a> with <a class="null" href="https://people.com/music/who-is-jutes-demi-lovato/" data-type="" data-component="link" data-source="inlineLink" data-ordinal="2" rel="noopener noreferrer">Jordan “Jutes” Lutes</a>, 35, on May 25, 2025, insisted that “communication” was the “biggest and the most important thing in a relationship.” 
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_7-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"><div id="mm-ads-native-fluid_1-0" class="comp mm-ads-native-fluid mm-ads-native " style="--native-ad-height: auto" data-right-rail-index="2"><div id="mm-ads-native__adunit_1-0" class="comp mm-ads-native__adunit mm-ads-gpt-dynamic-adunit mm-ads-gpt-adunit scads-to-load gpt native js-immediate-ad js-immediate-ad-loaded">

<p id="mntl-sc-block_9-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> “When you’re able to communicate with each other what you need, what you want, it creates a safe space for the two of you to share your feelings with one another,” Lovato tells PEOPLE.
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_10-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_11-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> “My love for Jordan grows every single day, and I’ve never been so happy in my life. So I think communication is a big part of that,” the star adds.
</p>

gold_text: Lovato opened up about her husband, Jutes, at the premiere of ‘Camp Rock 3’ in Burbank, Calif. on Monday, August 10. Demi Lovato is reflecting on the secret to her happy marriage! While attending the premiere of Camp Rock 3 at the Walt Disney Studio lot in Burbank, Calif., on Monday, Aug. 10, Lovato — who is reprising her role of Mitchie Torres, as well as acting as executive producer alongside the Jonas Brothers, in the upcoming film — spoke to PEOPLE about her recent one-year anniversary. Lovato, 33, who tied the knot with Jordan Jutes Lutes, 35, on May 25, 2025, insisted that communication was the biggest and the most important thing in a relationship. When you’re able to communicate with each other what you need, what you want, it creates a safe space for the two of you to share your feelings with one another, Lovato tells PEOPLE. My love for Jordan grows every single day, and I’ve never been so happy in my life. So I think communication is a big part of that, the star adds. Lovato and Lutes wed last May in a romantic California ceremony, according to Vogue, with the outlet also noting that the actress wore a custom pearl white Vivienne Westwood gown with a corset bodice and a cathedral-style tulle veil. When I was thinking about [what dress style I wanted], I often found myself coming back to Vivienne’s designs — specifically how the silhouettes really complement the curves in your body, and her use of corsets, Lovato told Vogue. Ahead of their big day, Lovato expressed her excitement to marry Lutes via a sweet Valentine’s Day post shared on Feb. 14 of that year. Jordan, I cannot WAIT to marry you!! The past 3 years have been the best 3 years of my life and I have you to thank for that, Lovato wrote at the time. I’m obsessed with your heart, your love and your light. I can’t wait to grow old with you and start a family together. Lutes and Lovato first went public with their romance in August 2022, with a source telling PEOPLE at the time that their relationship was really happy and healthy. Lutes then popped the question in a personal and intimate proposal in Los Angeles on Dec. 16, 2023, PEOPLE previously confirmed exclusively. In September 2024, Lovato told PEOPLE she’d waited [her] whole life for Lutes. It’s very grounding to have a partner that is so supportive, so loving, so caring. It’s very easy to stay centered with him because I love him so much and he treats me so amazing, she added of the singer. Camp Rock 3 premieres Aug. 13 on Disney Channel and will be streaming the next day on Disney+.

<div id="article-content_1-0" class="comp article-content mntl-block"><div id="mntl-sc-page_1-0" class="comp mntl-sc-page mntl-block structured-content" data-sc-sticky-offset="90" data-sc-ad-label-height="24" data-sc-ad-track-spacing="100" data-sc-min-track-height="250" data-sc-max-track-height="600" data-sc-breakpoint="50em" data-sc-load-immediate="4" data-sc-content-positions="[1, 1250, 1550, 1950, 2350, 2750, 3150, 3550, 3950]" data-bind-scroll-on-start="true"><div id="mntl-sc-block_1-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block people-sc-block-callout mntl-sc-block-universal-callout theme-needtoknow" data-tracking-id="mntl-sc-block-callout" data-tracking-container="true"> <h3 class="mntl-sc-block-universal-callout__heading">NEED TO KNOW</h3>
<div class="mntl-sc-block-universal-callout__body"><ul><li>Acclaimed author Mike Chen is releasing his debut young adult novel <em>Of Sorcery and Science</em> this fall</li><li>The story follows Andy Lao, a teen balancing high school life and his role as a magical realm’s Chosen One</li><li>PEOPLE can share an exclusive excerpt from <em>Of Sorcery and Science</em></li></ul></div>
</div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_2-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> Mike Chen is sharing a new magical story.
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_3-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_4-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> The acclaimed author, known for novels like <a class="null" href="https://bookshop.org/a/114093/9780778386940" data-component="link" data-source="inlineLink" data-type="externalLink" data-ordinal="1" rel="sponsored nofollow noskim noopener" target="_blank" data-caes-processed="true"><em>Light Years from Home</em></a> and his work for franchises like <em>Star Wars</em> and Marvel, is releasing his debut young adult novel this year.
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_5-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_6-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> <a class="null" href="https://www.barnesandnoble.com/w/of-sorcery-and-science-mike-chen/1149100926" data-component="link" data-source="inlineLink" data-type="externalLink" data-ordinal="1" rel="sponsored nofollow noskim noopener" target="_blank" data-caes-processed="true"><em>Of Sorcery and Science</em></a>, out this fall from Running Press, centers on Andy Lao, a teen who has just had the adventure of a lifetime. Months earlier, Andy accidentally entered a magical portal, became a mage and saved the realm, but no one at home believed him. Now, Andy is living a double life as both The Chosen One and a high schooler, struggling through math and science.
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_7-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_8-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> But when a mysterious girl comes through the portal claiming <em>she’s</em> The Chosen One, and that Andy put the realm at risk, they must work together to save it with science.
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_9-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>

<p id="mntl-sc-block_11-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> “I’ve always loved thinking about what happens to characters <em>after</em> their big adventure, because we’ve all faced that letdown when returning to normal life, right?” Chen says of the novel’s inception. “<a class="null" href="https://www.amazon.com/Sorcery-Science-Mike-chen/dp/B0GDZZPZRG/?tag=people-onsite-prod-20&ascsubtag=12058538%7C%7C%7C%7C%7C%7Cpc" data-component="amazon" data-source="affiliate" data-type="externalLink" data-ordinal="1" rel="sponsored nofollow noskim noopener" data-aps-asin="B0GDZZPZRG" data-aps-asc-tag="{NCA_TAG}" data-aps-asc-subtag="{NCA_SUBTAG}" target="_blank" data-caes-processed="true"><em>Of Sorcery and Science</em></a> lets me play with that to the most extreme example, with a high schooler whose heroic quest in a magical realm still doesn’t help him prepare for college applications or trig tests.”
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_12-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_13-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> Chen also hopes the book is relatable for young readers who may related to Andy’s journey.
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_14-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_15-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> “For teen readers, I hope they can identify with that sense of feeling a little out of place between two worlds (metaphorically or real!) — and I hope they come away realizing that their greatest strength comes from navigating those worlds their own way,” he says.
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_16-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>

<p id="mntl-sc-block_22-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> <em>Julia had so little mana left, what was the worst that could happen? I steeled myself against possibly needing to push my parents out of the way of a fireball.</em>
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_23-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_24-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> <em>“You go ahead,” my dad said. “We respect you.”</em>
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_25-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_26-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> <em>“You don’t need to join me in prayer,” she said, though my dad bowed his head anyway, shortly followed by my mom. We sat and looked at each other, mutual shrugs each way, and then Julia began mumbling.</em>
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_27-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_28-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> <em>I heard bits and pieces through her lowered voice, and caught the distinctive bits of the Heal incantation. Which — considering that the last time she tried it, a Magic Missile got launched into the sky — might not have been the best idea.</em>
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_29-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_30-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> <em>She finished the incantation, and a moment after the final words came out, the extra green mana drained from her fingertips. Really, everything about her demeanor changed, like she’d just woken from a nap.</em>
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_31-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_32-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> <em>Maybe green mana only backfired on the initial spell, but residual energy processed as planned. That didn’t really make much sense to me, but if it worked, it worked.</em>
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_33-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_34-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> <em>“Okay, I’m good. Thanks,” she said, picking up the pizza. “I’m hungry. I haven’t had pizza in a while.”</em>
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_35-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_36-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> <em>Julia took one bite, then two, letting out an “mmm” as she chomped down. On the other side of the table, my parents continued to sit with heads bowed. For the next few seconds, the only sound came from Julia eating way too loudly. Yet, what followed was . . .</em>
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_37-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_38-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> <em>Well, I’d never seen anything like it.</em>
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_39-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>

<p id="mntl-sc-block_42-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> <em>It started like a repressed sneeze from my dad, a sort of explosive squeak from his sinuses. Julia even said “bless you” through her pizza. Except when I looked at him, his head stayed bowed, his eyes squeezed shut tighter than I’d ever seen, and the impossible happened.</em>
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_43-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_44-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> <em>My often silent, very stoic dad </em>cried<em>.</em>
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_45-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_46-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> <em>Not a lot. This was, like, several drops leaking out from the corners of his eyes. His shoulders shook, and soon my mom followed suit too. “Andy,” he finally said, his voice with a very unusually low gravel, “do you know why we came to America?”</em>
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_47-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_48-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> <em>“Uh . . .” I started while meeting Julia’s gaze, my wide stare giving away that none of this was expected. “Because —”</em>
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_49-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_50-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> <em>“You have never seen poverty until you see the slums back home,” he said. “Nothing in America comes close. America has its problems. Too much time arguing about culture. But it comes with opportunity. I wish more Americans realize that. They take it for granted.”</em>
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_51-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_52-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> <em>My parents almost never talked about politics, except about the local school board elections. They certainly never talked about, well, “culture.”</em>
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_53-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_54-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block people-sc-block-callout mntl-sc-block-universal-callout theme-generic" data-tracking-id="mntl-sc-block-callout" data-tracking-container="true">
<div class="mntl-sc-block-universal-callout__body"><p>Never miss a story — sign up for <a class="null" href="https://people.com/people-news-daily-newsletter-sign-up-8692701" data-component="link" data-source="inlineLink" data-type="internalLink" data-ordinal="1" rel="noopener">PEOPLE’s free daily newsletter</a> to stay up-to-date on the best of what PEOPLE has to offer, from celebrity news to compelling human interest stories.</p></div>
</div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_55-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> <em>“Sometimes,” my mom said, “we worry that you take everything for granted. Everything we did was to give this life to you. You can’t let opportunity pass you by. Grades are so important. We worry so much that you don’t see it.”</em>
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_56-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_57-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> <em>They </em>worried<em>.</em><br><br><em>No, that wasn’t it.</em>
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_58-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_59-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> <em>Julia mouthed the word “fear” at me.</em>
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_60-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_61-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> <em>Her attempt to drain the last bit of magic had backfired into a Fear spell. And now my parents experienced their worst fears: They talked about their </em>feelings<em> with me.</em>
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_62-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_63-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> <em>Julia shook her hands at me, then gestured for me to say </em>something<em>. Probably a good idea. I didn’t need my parents to run out screaming like what happened when she cast it on those lacrosse players. “I understand,” I said slowly, mostly so I could stall and come up with something brilliant to snap them out of it. “I know you had hard lives growing up. I . . . do appreciate that.”</em>
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_64-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_65-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> <em>Now Julia’s hands waved in a rolling motion, and I realized that I’d never actually cast a Fear spell, so I had no idea how someone was supposed to break the spell. What was the one thing I could say to my parents at this moment of them being, like, actual vulnerable humans? Non-Asian parents in TV shows talked about this stuff all the time, yet my parents were living stereotypes. In just a few sentences, I understood </em>why<em> much better.</em>
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_66-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_67-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block people-sc-block-callout mntl-sc-block-universal-callout theme-generic" data-tracking-id="mntl-sc-block-callout" data-tracking-container="true">
<div class="mntl-sc-block-universal-callout__body"><p>Need your next page-turner? </div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_68-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> <em>I thought about parents and teens on TV and what they said to one another before they gave deep, meaningful hugs.</em>
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_69-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_70-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> <em>“I’m sorry for disappointing you,” I finally said.</em>
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_71-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_72-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> <em>And just like that, my parents straightened up. My dad sniffled, and my mom wiped her eyes.</em>
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_73-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_74-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-html"> <em>“Bad allergy day,” she said, before looking at Julia. </em>“So, what you write your USC application essay on?”
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_75-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>

gold_text: The author hopes young readers identify with that sense of feeling a little out of place between two worlds. Mike Chen is sharing a new magical story. The acclaimed author, known for novels like Light Years from Home and his work for franchises like Star Wars and Marvel, is releasing his debut young adult novel this year. Of Sorcery and Science, out this fall from Running Press, centers on Andy Lao, a teen who has just had the adventure of a lifetime. Months earlier, Andy accidentally entered a magical portal, became a mage and saved the realm, but no one at home believed him. Now, Andy is living a double life as both The Chosen One and a high schooler, struggling through math and science. But when a mysterious girl comes through the portal claiming she’s The Chosen One, and that Andy put the realm at risk, they must work together to save it with science. I’ve always loved thinking about what happens to characters after their big adventure, because we’ve all faced that letdown when returning to normal life, right? Chen says of the novel’s inception. Of Sorcery and Science lets me play with that to the most extreme example, with a high schooler whose heroic quest in a magical realm still doesn’t help him prepare for college applications or trig tests. Chen also hopes the book is relatable for young readers who may related to Andy’s journey. For teen readers, I hope they can identify with that sense of feeling a little out of place between two worlds (metaphorically or real!) — and I hope they come away realizing that their greatest strength comes from navigating those worlds their own way, he says. Read an excerpt from Of Sorcery and Science below. Julia had so little mana left, what was the worst that could happen? I steeled myself against possibly needing to push my parents out of the way of a fireball. You go ahead, my dad said. We respect you. You don’t need to join me in prayer, she said, though my dad bowed his head anyway, shortly followed by my mom. We sat and looked at each other, mutual shrugs each way, and then Julia began mumbling. I heard bits and pieces through her lowered voice, and caught the distinctive bits of the Heal incantation. Which — considering that the last time she tried it, a Magic Missile got launched into the sky — might not have been the best idea. She finished the incantation, and a moment after the final words came out, the extra green mana drained from her fingertips. Really, everything about her demeanor changed, like she’d just woken from a nap. Maybe green mana only backfired on the initial spell, but residual energy processed as planned. That didn’t really make much sense to me, but if it worked, it worked. Okay, I’m good. Thanks, she said, picking up the pizza. I’m hungry. I haven’t had pizza in a while. Julia took one bite, then two, letting out an mmm as she chomped down. On the other side of the table, my parents continued to sit with heads bowed. For the next few seconds, the only sound came from Julia eating way too loudly. Yet, what followed was . . . Well, I’d never seen anything like it. It started like a repressed sneeze from my dad, a sort of explosive squeak from his sinuses. Julia even said bless you through her pizza. Except when I looked at him, his head stayed bowed, his eyes squeezed shut tighter than I’d ever seen, and the impossible happened. My often silent, very stoic dad cried. Not a lot. This was, like, several drops leaking out from the corners of his eyes. His shoulders shook, and soon my mom followed suit too. Andy, he finally said, his voice with a very unusually low gravel, do you know why we came to America? Uh . . . I started while meeting Julia’s gaze, my wide stare giving away that none of this was expected. Because — You have never seen poverty until you see the slums back home, he said. Nothing in America comes close. America has its problems. Too much time arguing about culture. But it comes with opportunity. I wish more Americans realize that. They take it for granted. My parents almost never talked about politics, except about the local school board elections. They certainly never talked about, well, culture. Sometimes, my mom said, we worry that you take everything for granted. Everything we did was to give this life to you. You can’t let opportunity pass you by. Grades are so important. We worry so much that you don’t see it. They worried. No, that wasn’t it. Julia mouthed the word fear at me. Her attempt to drain the last bit of magic had backfired into a Fear spell. And now my parents experienced their worst fears: They talked about their feelings with me. Julia shook her hands at me, then gestured for me to say something. Probably a good idea. I didn’t need my parents to run out screaming like what happened when she cast it on those lacrosse players. I understand, I said slowly, mostly so I could stall and come up with something brilliant to snap them out of it. I know you had hard lives growing up. I . . . do appreciate that. Now Julia’s hands waved in a rolling motion, and I realized that I’d never actually cast a Fear spell, so I had no idea how someone was supposed to break the spell. What was the one thing I could say to my parents at this moment of them being, like, actual vulnerable humans? Non-Asian parents in TV shows talked about this stuff all the time, yet my parents were living stereotypes. In just a few sentences, I understood why much better. I thought about parents and teens on TV and what they said to one another before they gave deep, meaningful hugs. I’m sorry for disappointing you, I finally said. And just like that, my parents straightened up. My dad sniffled, and my mom wiped her eyes. Bad allergy day, she said, before looking at Julia. So, what you write your USC application essay on?
